result.summary: Pausanias continues listing victor statues at Olympia, giving the victors' feats and who set up the statues. The longest entry covers the Theban Clitomachus and his loss to Caprus of Elis, who won wrestling and pancratium on the same day. Statues of kings and rulers given as offerings are also noted.

scenes.title: Statues of boxers, runners and others
scenes.summary: Pausanias lists victors such as Archippus, Xenon, Clinomachus, Pantarches, Olidas, Charinus and Ageles, with their sculptors or dedicators.

scenes.title: Clitomachus of Thebes and Caprus
scenes.summary: Clitomachus's record is given, then how he asked for the pancratium to be called before the boxing and lost to Caprus.
scenes.stakes: Clitomachus risks losing the pancratium prize by exhaustion from fighting several events in one day.

scenes.title: More victors, kings and rulers
scenes.summary: Statues of Epitherses, Hiero, Timoptolis, Archidamus, Demetrius, Antigonus, Eutelidas, Areus, Gorgus, Ptolemy and Caprus are described.

notable_quotes.reason: Clitomachus's tactical request shows the rules and strategy of combined events.

analysis.text: The passage shows the Greek honour given to athletic victory, recorded through statues, feats and civic pride.
Statues of kings and tyrants beside athletes show how cities and rulers used Olympia to display status and diplomacy.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias's lists preserve names of victors and sculptors that are otherwise unknown, making him a key source for Olympic history.

language_notes.text: "Beat all comers" means he defeated every opponent; the Pythian, Nemean and Isthmian games with Olympia made up the four major festivals, the 'circuit'.
Pentathlum: the five-event contest (running, jumping, discus, javelin, wrestling).
Double course (diaulos): a race of two stadium lengths, down and back.
Pancratium: a brutal combined contest of wrestling and boxing with very few rules.
"Battered about by boxing": Clitomachus wanted the pancratium first, so he would not be exhausted by the boxing beforehand.
"A man like a hunter" is a vague description of a separate statue, showing a figure dressed or posed as a hunter.
"Were let any one know votive offerings" is garbled in this translation; it means the statues were dedications by the Byzantians.
The note says boys' events were called before the men's, with the pentathlum called last.

context_notes.text: The Achæans were a league of Peloponnesian cities; Elis, the host of Olympia, was often entangled in their wars.
Hiero the son of Dinomenes was the famous early tyrant of Syracuse, celebrated in Pindar's victory odes.
Demetrius Poliorcetes was captured by Seleucus; Antigonus (Gonatas) was his son. Byzantium was a Greek city on the Bosporus.
Areus was a Spartan king of the third century BC.
Ptolemy son of Lagus was the general of Alexander who became king of Egypt.

literary_notes.text: Clitomachus's tactical request backfires: he gets the order he wanted yet loses to Caprus.
Clitomachus's 'stout heart and untired body' shows his courage, ironically undone by his own clever request.
Pausanias refers back to his earlier account, tying the catalogue together like a guide who knows his route.
